ahub: A CLI that runs configured AI agents non-interactively.
one_liner: Run a configured agent from the command line, non-interactively, with the conversation stored durably in bkn.

model.where_state_lives: In a bkn instance, in three owner-scoped collections (hub/agents, hub/threads, hub/messages). ahub keeps only a profile on disk: a bkn URL, your token, and a provider key.
model.what_it_is_not: Not a chat UI and not a daemon. No RAG: context comes from memgraph memories and skills, which are written on purpose and readable as text. No sub-agents, HITL or workflows yet.
model.context: Two optional blocks are prepended as system messages before a turn: recalled memories (reference material, from a memgraph project) and skills (procedures, named explicitly). Both are reported on the answer, so a turn given without them never looks like one given with them.
model.tools: An agent may be given tools, and then a turn becomes a loop: the model asks for a tool, the result goes back to it, and it answers. Tools are opt-in per agent or per call, the memory and skill tools need memgraph while cmd and the job tools need an allowlist, and anything that writes needs --allow-writes as well.
model.flows: A flow is a path expressed as data: steps, a start, and where each goes next. Most step types cost nothing -- collect a value, branch on it, run an allowlisted CLI, call an allowlisted host -- and exactly one (ask) calls a model. A run pauses when it needs input and is resumed by id, so a wizard works in a tool that must never prompt.
model.agents: An agent is a saved configuration: a system prompt, a model, and optionally a memory project, skills and tools. It is the noun this tool is named after. `ahub chat --agent <name>` talks to one; a flow's ask step calls one; a schedule runs one unattended.
model.schedules: A schedule is a standing instruction: run this agent, on this cadence, with nobody watching. Each run starts a FRESH thread and carries forward one bounded note -- the scratchpad -- that the agent writes itself. Replaying history would make every run cost more than the last and eventually stop fitting; a note cannot.
model.what_it_is: An agent is a saved prompt + model. A thread is a conversation with one agent. A chat is one turn. A flow is a deterministic path. A schedule runs an agent unattended.
model.evals: An eval is a set of cases with assertions, run against an agent, producing a pass rate and a cost. It is how a prompt, model, memory or tool change stops being an opinion. Most assertions are free to check; exactly one (judge) asks a model, and the report says how much that cost.
model.jobs: A job is a permitted command running outside the turn that started it. A turn cannot wait: a test suite or a deploy outlives the provider timeout. A job survives the process that began it, so a schedule can start something and a later run collect it.
model.compaction: Threads grow. Every response reports prompt_tokens, so the size is measured rather than estimated, and a thread is folded into a summary once it crosses a fraction of the model's window (60% by default). If the provider refuses a prompt anyway, the window it names is learned and written to the profile, the thread is folded, and the turn is retried once.

loop: ahub setup --admin-token <t>  # Once per bkn instance, by a human. Declares the collections and their owner-scoped access policy. Never needed again, and never run on the serving path.

ahub login --email --password

# Stores a user token in the active profile. Every later call carries this token, so bkn decides what you can see.
ahub agent create --name helper --model <m> --system "..."  # Saves the configuration once so later turns are one short command.
ahub chat --agent helper --message "..."  # Opens a thread and answers. Prints the thread id; pass it back with --thread to continue.
ahub chat --agent helper --thread <id> --message "..."  # Continues an existing conversation. History is replayed to the model automatically.
ahub thread show <id>  # The full transcript, in order, with per-message token counts.

ahub agent update helper --memory-project

--skills a,b # Gives an agent a memory scope and a set of procedures. Both are opt-in and both are named in the configuration, so an answer can be reproduced from it.

ahub memory recall --query "..." --project

# Read memgraph directly, rendered through the same budget a chat turn would use, so you see what the model would see.
ahub skill recommend "<task>"  # Ask memgraph's skill graph which procedure fits, then `ahub skill show <name>` to read it before spending tokens on it.
ahub tool list  # What a model can be given. Needs no token and no backend: discover the surface before wiring anything.
ahub chat --agent helper --tools memory_recall,skill_show --message "..."  # Let the model look things up for itself. The answer reports steps and tool_runs, so you can see what it actually did.
ahub flow validate --file f.json  # Because the path is data it can be checked before it costs anything: unknown targets, unreachable steps, variables nothing sets, commands this machine will refuse.
ahub flow run <name> --input k=v  # Runs until it ends or needs input. Exit 92 means it paused and names what it needs; exit 105 means a step failed. The run reports steps, llm_calls and tokens.
ahub flow resume <run-id> --input k=v  # Continue a paused run. The run is stored in bkn, so this works from another machine or another day.
ahub install  # Copy the binary you already have to ~/.local/bin. Idempotent, no sudo, and it never edits your shell profile.
ahub update [--check]  # Fetch the published build. The version is sha256[:12] of the artifact, so there is no number to bump: identical bytes are the same version.

ahub schedule create --name nightly --agent helper --prompt "..." --every 6h  # A standing instruction. --every <duration> or --at HH:MM; anything more elaborate is a systemd timer calling `ahub schedule run <name>`.
ahub schedule tick  # Runs everything that is due. This is what a timer calls: one entry point, however many schedules, no daemon holding state between them.
ahub eval validate --file quality.json  # Every regex compiles and every bound parses before a single token is spent finding out otherwise.

ahub eval run quality [--strict]  # Scores an agent, case by case, on stderr as it goes. Exits 0 however it scored; --strict exits 1 when assertions failed, for a pipeline or a schedule that should go red.

ahub eval create --from-thread <id> --name <eval> --expect not_contains=probably  # Turns a bad run into a case. It must fail on that thread, or it is refused. Running it uses the thread's tools again.
ahub eval compare <before> <after>  # The only question that matters after a change: what got fixed, what regressed, what still fails, and what it cost.
ahub job start --command 'gh pr list' && ahub job wait <id>  # Work that outlives a turn. job list, job output and job stop are there too.
ahub model list  # Context windows, shared through bkn. One machine learns a window from a refused call and the rest already know it.
ahub spend  # What today has cost against the day's allowance. The counter is in bkn (a fact), the allowance is in the profile (a decision).

examples.goal: The answer alone, for a pipeline.
The five most recently touched conversations with one agent.
Watch the answer arrive while still getting a parseable stream.
One turn with recalled context, without changing the saved agent.
do: ahub chat --agent helper --memory-project machin --message "why does the daemon loop leak?"

examples.goal: Load a procedure for one turn.
do: ahub chat --agent helper --skill agent-first-cli-specs --message "audit this exit code table"

examples.goal: The answer plus exactly what informed it.
The answer plus the path it took to get there.
do: ahub chat --agent agent --tools memory_recall --message '...' | jq '{answer:.content, steps, tools:[.tool_runs[].name]}'

examples.goal: Where the money went: five deterministic steps and one model call.
do: ahub flow run release-notes --input repo=~/ai/agents-hub | jq '{steps, llm_calls, tokens}'

examples.goal: Run a scheduled flow by hand and read its history back out of bkn.
do: ahub flow run bkn-backup && ahub flow runs --flow bkn-backup --limit 5

examples.goal: What one autonomous run did, and what it cost.
do: ahub schedule run nightly | jq '{status, steps, tokens, wrote:.scratchpad_written}'

examples.goal: An agent reaching a real system, through a command shape you chose.
do: ahub config set --allow-tool-cmd 'gh pr list' && ahub chat --agent helper --tools cmd --message 'what PRs are open?'

examples.goal: An ops flow with no model in it at all: measure the journal, compare against a budget, vacuum only when told to.
do: ahub flow run log-budget   # measure, branch, act; llm_calls: 0

concepts.owner scoping: bkn stamps every document with your user id from your token and filters reads by it. ahub never sends an owner field, so it cannot read or write another user's threads even if this code has a bug.
concepts.provider: Any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint: OpenAI, Mistral, Ollama, vLLM, OpenRouter. Set it once with `ahub config set --provider-url ... --provider-key ...`.
concepts.profile: A named set of {bkn url, token, provider, model}, like an aws-cli profile. Switch with --profile or `ahub config set-profile <n>`.
concepts.seq: Messages are ordered by an integer seq, not by timestamp, so two messages written in the same millisecond can never come back swapped.
concepts.memory: Recall is delegated to the memgraph CLI: explicit argv, no shell, validated values, a timeout and a character budget. ahub implements no retrieval of its own and stores no embeddings.
concepts.skills: A skill is a SKILL.md resolved by name through memgraph's skill graph. ahub reads only the file memgraph pointed at, only when the skill was named, and only if it is markdown.
concepts.budget: Recalled memories are capped per-memory and in total (default 1200/6000 characters). This is the difference between memory as a feature and memory as a bill, since the block is re-sent every turn.
concepts.the tool loop: Up to --max-steps (default 8) passes: each pass either answers or asks for tools, whose results are appended and fed back. Every agent and tool turn is stored, so a thread with tool calls resumes correctly.
concepts.two gates on writes: Naming a tool enables it; a tool that changes state needs --allow-writes too. 'Give it tools' and 'let it change things' are different decisions and one flag would collapse them.
concepts.flow vs agent: An agent improvises and pays per turn; a flow follows a path someone designed and pays only for its ask steps. Use a flow when the sequence is known and must be reproducible, an agent when it is not.
concepts.allowlists: cmd and http steps can only reach commands and hosts allowed in the local profile, never ones named by the flow. A flow is data -- possibly data a model wrote -- so a flow that could name its own executables would be arbitrary code execution with extra steps.
concepts.derived variables: A cmd or http step sets three: the output, <var>_code (exit status or HTTP status) and <var>_err. Branching on a cli-output-spec exit code is the point: 105 retry, 82 fix the arguments, 92 not there.
concepts.secrets: Referenced as {{secret.NAME}} and resolved from the local profile, so a definition can be stored and shared without its credentials. Values are redacted before anything is written to a run.
concepts.script steps: A script step runs a bkn script with YOUR token. bkn decides whether it may run, per script, next to the code being run -- so this tool needs no allowlist for it. An operator opens one with `bkn script update <name> --run-access user`. The script sees bkn.caller, so it can scope what it returns to whoever asked.
concepts.scheduled flows: A flow plus a systemd timer is the whole of autonomy: `ahub flow run <name>` on a schedule, no daemon and no user in the loop. The flow exits non-zero when a step fails, so a failure shows up in `systemctl list-units --failed`, and every run is recorded in bkn where `ahub flow runs` can read it back.
concepts.the scratchpad: One bounded note (4000 chars) carried between runs, written by the agent through the scratchpad tool and readable or correctable by a human with `ahub schedule scratchpad <name>`. Durable knowledge goes to memgraph via memory_save instead; the scratchpad is only 'where I got to last time'.
concepts.agent vs flow: A flow is a path someone designed and pays only for its ask steps. A schedule lets an agent decide what to do, on a cadence, and pays every run. Reach for a flow when the sequence is known; a schedule when it is not.
concepts.agent vs schedule: The agent is the configuration; the schedule is the standing instruction that runs it. One agent can carry several schedules with different prompts and cadences.
concepts.assertions: contains, not_contains, equals, matches, max_tokens, max_steps, tool_used, tool_not_used and judge. All free except judge, which asks a second agent for a PASS/FAIL and a reason. Name a separate judge agent: a model grading its own homework is a weaker signal than a second one.
concepts.the cmd tool: Lets an agent run commands, but only shapes an operator wrote down: `ahub config set --allow-tool-cmd 'gh pr list'`. The model picks a permitted prefix and can never change it. A prefix alone takes no arguments: each further one must match a pattern listed with `ahub config set --allow-tool-arg 'git log --oneline --since=*'`, where * is any text but never admits a flag unless the pattern starts with '-'. A command gets a minimal environment (PATH, HOME, locale, TZ and similar); name any other variable it needs with `ahub config set --allow-env GH_TOKEN`, which applies to every command. This is not a sandbox: a command runs as your user and can read what you can. Empty by default, which means the tool does not exist until someone permits something.
concepts.jobs: Started through the same prefix allowlist as the cmd tool, so a human starting one by hand is bound by what this machine permits a model to run. A model gets three verbs -- job_start, job_wait, job_output -- and cannot list or stop work it did not begin.
concepts.compaction: Folds the older half of a thread into a summary stored on the thread. The messages are never deleted: replay skips what the summary covers, but the record of what was said survives for anyone who later needs to know why an agent did something.
concepts.how deterministic a flow is: The control flow is: no step but ask calls a model, the operators are a closed set, first match wins, and an unset {{variable}} fails the step rather than substituting empty. A run reports llm_calls and tokens, so 'this costs nothing' is checkable rather than claimed. What is NOT deterministic is what the commands say -- that is the point of asking them.
concepts.privileged steps: Do not run ahub as root. Allowlist the privileged SHAPE instead: `--allow-cmd 'sudo journalctl'` permits journalctl as root and nothing else, because the allowlist matches whole-field prefixes. The real gate is the sudoers rule, which the OS enforces and audits; ahub's allowlist is the second one. For anything genuinely dangerous, put the work in a root-owned systemd unit and let the flow only start it -- then a compromised ahub can trigger one predefined action, not compose a new one.
concepts.what lives where: bkn holds everything that should travel: agents, threads, flows, schedules, evals, jobs, and what has been learned about models. The local profile holds what should NOT travel -- your token, your provider key, your secrets, and the allowlists -- because a credential and a capability grant are policies of one machine, and a new machine must not inherit them by logging in. memgraph holds memories and skills in its own store.
concepts.guards for unattended work: A schedule takes a lease before it runs, so a timer and a slow run cannot overlap, and so does a thread, so two turns cannot weave into one conversation (exit 95 thread_busy). A lease left by a process that died on this machine is taken over at once; one held elsewhere expires 30m after its last renewal. A tick also reaps jobs whose supervisor is gone. `ahub job prune` removes finished jobs and their output. A daily token budget refuses a turn BEFORE it spends, counted atomically in bkn. A flow has its own deadline as well as a per-step one.

gotchas: The user message is stored before the model is called. A provider timeout costs you the answer, not the question: retry with the same --thread.
--stream writes JSON Lines: start (thread id), delta, tool_call, tool_result, then the envelope with type result. A failed turn has no result line; resume the thread start named.
An agent name that matches two agents is an error, not a coin flip. Use the id, or rename one.
Exit 105 means the model provider failed and a retry may work. Exit 90 means your token is wrong or expired and retrying will not help.
`ahub setup` needs the bkn ADMIN token; nothing else does. If a command asks you for the admin token, that is a bug.
Deleting an agent leaves its threads: a conversation that happened is a fact, and dropping the config does not un-happen it.
Memories are framed as reference material and the model is told not to follow instructions inside them. Skills are the opposite: they ARE instructions, which is why one is only loaded when named.

A memory or skill that cannot be loaded degrades the turn instead of failing it, and says so in the answer's `memory.error` / `skills.skipped`. Pass --memory-required or --skills-required to make it fatal.
Several servers behind the OpenAI wire shape keep only the FIRST system message; ahub merges the leading run into one, which is what makes an injected memory block actually arrive.
The provider timeout is separate from the bkn timeout (AHUB_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT, default 300s). A reasoning model with a large prompt will exceed a database-shaped timeout.
An expired access token is refreshed and re-persisted automatically -- but only for a token that came from the profile. A token passed in by --token or AHUB_TOKEN is yours to manage.
A tool failure is returned to the model as the tool's result, not raised. It can then try something else, and the failure is still visible in tool_runs[].failed.
Running out of steps with no answer is exit 105 (max_steps_exhausted), not a successful empty answer. The thread is stored: resume it with --thread and a bigger --max-steps.

memory_recall defaults its project to the agent's memory_project. Without that a model omits the project (it reads as context, not a parameter), every call fails, and it retries the same shape until the cap.
Usage is summed across every step of the loop, not just the last call.
A flow run that needs input exits 92 (needs_input) with the run id and the exact resume command. That is not a failure; a failed step is exit 105.
An unset {{variable}} fails the step instead of substituting an empty string: a command with a silently empty argument is a different command.
Command arguments are argv, never a shell line. A collected value containing `;` or backticks stays one argument.
An allowlist problem is a warning at validate time and a refusal at run time -- a definition has to stay storable on a machine that cannot run it.
A conditional with no else ends the run when nothing matches, rather than guessing a branch.

bkn answers a script you may not run exactly as it answers one that does not exist, so that 404s cannot enumerate what an operator installed. A refusal therefore names both possibilities; it is not being vague, it genuinely cannot tell you which.
A bkn script that runs and throws is a RESULT, not a transport failure: the step sets <var>_code=1 and takes on_error, so a flow can handle it.

update verifies the download against the advertised hash AND runs it before swapping. A hash mismatch or a binary that will not run exits 110 and leaves the working binary untouched -- neither is worth retrying, because the published bytes are wrong.
A machine account needs a credential that outlives its tokens: the refresh token is good for 30 days, so a timer that runs at least monthly never needs the password again, and one that lapses does.
A scheduled run never replays previous runs. If it needs to remember something, it must write the scratchpad or save a memory -- and it can only do that if it was given the tools.
The scratchpad tool is always offered inside a scheduled run and is not subject to --allow-writes: it can only overwrite that one schedule's own note.
A failed run still advances the schedule. An agent that stopped rescheduling when it broke would go quiet exactly when you needed it to keep complaining.
`ahub schedule tick` exits 105 if any schedule failed, so a timer that always exits 0 does not hide a broken agent. The successful runs are recorded either way.
Re-enabling a disabled schedule computes a fresh due time rather than firing once for every slot it slept through.
An eval runs an agent with its real memory, skills and tools. Measuring it without them would measure a different agent than the one that answers real questions.
Each case gets a fresh thread, so a case cannot be influenced by the one above it in the file.
A case whose model call failed counts as FAILED, never skipped: an outage must never read as an improvement.

`ahub eval run` exits 0 whatever it scored -- the code says the eval ran, the data says how it went. --strict exits 1, deliberately outside cli-output-spec's 80-119 bands, because the tool worked and the agent did not. 105 would tell an agent to retry a failing eval and expect a different answer.
A judge assertion with no judge configured FAILS rather than passing: a check that silently becomes a no-op is worse than no check.

The cmd tool has its own allowlist, separate from a flow's --allow-cmd. A flow step runs argv a human wrote; the cmd tool runs argv a model wrote, so it allowlists PREFIXES rather than bare command names, and a prefix takes no further arguments until --allow-tool-arg lists them. If a command is refused for its arguments, an operator has to permit them.
cmd is not behind --allow-writes, deliberately: the prefix list is a stronger and more specific gate, and a flag you must pass even to run `git log` teaches people the flag means nothing.
The result a model sees starts with the exit code, because that is the part worth branching on -- and every tool in this ecosystem follows the same convention.
A job's exit code survives because the process ahub spawns is ahub itself, supervising the command. Spawning the command directly would leave nobody to reap it once the turn exits.
Compaction is reported on the turn that did it (`compaction` in the answer), never silent. A conversation that quietly lost its middle would be impossible to debug.

A thread is folded at most once per prompt size: if folding did not shrink the prompt, the size is coming from somewhere a summary cannot reach -- a large system prompt, a recalled block -- and folding again would cost another summarisation for nothing.
When a prompt cannot be made to fit at all, the error is exit 85 prompt_too_large rather than a retryable provider error, because the same prompt will not fit next time either.

A flow has no arithmetic. It can COMPARE numbers (gt/lt read the leading number, so `du -sb` output compares straight against a budget) but it cannot compute one. If you need a calculation, do it in the command.

A conditional reads its variable by name, so an unset one compares as empty rather than failing the way a template does. Declare optional variables in the flow's `inputs` list; anything else that no step sets is reported by validate.

An allowlist entry is a whole-field prefix: 'sudo journalctl' permits `sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=250M` and refuses `sudo rm`. A one-word entry behaves as it always did, allowing any arguments -- which is why 'sudo' alone should never be one.
A context window learned from a provider's refusal is written to bkn, not the profile: it is a fact about the model. An explicit --model-limit in the profile is an override and still wins.

A job's output tail (16 KB) is stored with its record so another machine can read it; the full log stays where it ran. `ahub job output` says which one you got -- "local file (complete)" or "recorded tail (portable)".

A schedule that appears not to run may be leased: tick reports it as skipped with held_by, and `ahub schedule run <name>` exits 95 naming the holder. A holder that died on this machine is replaced at once; one elsewhere is waited out for up to 30 minutes.
A thread cut off mid tool call can be resumed: replay tells the model the call was interrupted and may or may not have run. Check before repeating anything that writes.

The daily budget is checked before a turn, not after -- a budget enforced afterwards is a report. It refuses with exit 95 budget_spent, because the state conflicts with the request rather than the request being wrong.
`ahub flow run --timeout` bounds the whole flow; --step-timeout bounds one command. When a command is stopped, the error names which of the two clocks ran out.
`--help` or `-h` on any command prints its entry from help-json and runs nothing. A flag a command does not have is exit 80 unknown_flag, also before anything runs.

`ahub update --check` exits 5 when a different build is published, with the data on stdout. It compares content hashes, so a different build can be an older one. Builds are not signed: only update from a server you trust.
A release build checks for a newer one at most once a day, on commands that talk to a server, and says so on stderr. AHUB_NO_NUDGE=1 or CI turns it off. A build from source never checks.

`ahub feedback` sends your message, kind, context and the tool version to https://feedback.intrane.fr, and nothing unless you run it. Put no secrets in it. FEEDBACK_RELAY=off sends nothing. There is no telemetry.
